name: Individual false lashes / magnetic lashes

lead: False lashes add length and density to the lash line the moment they go on. Individual lashes are applied one by one by a technician, while magnetic lashes clamp on with small magnets and come off daily.

The synthetic lashes attach to or clamp around natural lashes, adding visible length and volume without changing the natural lash. Individual extensions last a few weeks. Artificial lashes date back more than a century, and magnetic versions were invented in 2014 as a glue-free option. No clinical studies were found.

paras: Individual lashes are booked with a technician and refilled periodically; magnetic lashes are put on at home for an occasion or daily and removed at night. Both are often paired with mascara or eyeliner.
Adhesives used for glued lashes can cause skin sensitivity in some people, and magnetic lashes may pose a hazard near MRI machines.

chain: Artificial lashes attach to lash line
angle.text: Users add strip, individual or magnetic lashes for instant length and volume. The artificial lashes attach to the lash line, so the fuller look is visible right away and temporary. No clinical research on the products was found.

lead: False eyelashes are artificial lashes attached to or near the natural lash line to add length, volume or density. Common forms are strip lashes, individual lash extensions applied one at a time by a technician, and magnetic lashes that clamp onto the natural lashes without glue.[1]

Artificial lashes date back more than a century: a 1902-1903 British patent by Karl Nessler and a 1911 US patent by Anna Taylor are recorded, and magnetic lashes were invented in 2014 by Katy Stoka as a glue-free alternative.[1] No clinical studies of individual or magnetic lashes were found.

paras: Strip lashes are synthetic, trimmable strips fixed above the natural lashes with temporary glue and removed with warm water or eye makeup remover.[1] Individual extensions are attached one by one to natural lashes with semi-permanent adhesive, usually by a technician over up to two hours, and last about three to four weeks.[1] Magnetic lashes use a magnetic strip that sandwiches the natural lashes, so no adhesive is needed, and they are reusable.[1]

A report from 1882 described Parisians sewing hair into the eyelids, and a 1899 newspaper account described a similar method as painful. Karl Nessler patented artificial lashes in the UK in 1902-1903, Anna Taylor patented a fabric-strip design in the US in 1911, and false lashes became popular in the early 1930s and again in the 1960s.[1] Magnetic lashes followed in 2014.[1]

Wikipedia notes that magnetic lashes may pose a hazard in MRI scanning rooms because of their magnets, and recounts that an actress's eyes swelled nearly shut after lashes were glued on for a 1916 film.[1] The page does not describe adhesive reactions in detail. A general review of contact dermatitis to cosmetics covers allergic reactions to cosmetic ingredients, though it does not address lashes specifically.
No studies found. Related laboratory work on lash cosmetics includes a 2020 formulation study of a curling mascara using a thermoresponsive polymer, which is not a study of false lashes.[2]
